newsitem.title: KENYA: FOCUS-Kenya shilling at record dlr low pre-strike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kenya shilling at record dlr low pre-strike.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling hit an official record low against the dollar on Thursday on sustained pressure from investors pulling out of the market and ahead of a national strike on Friday, commercial bank dealers said.
Kenyan markets have been jolted since the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a $205 million three-year aid package to Kenya a week ago in a row over corruption.

The shilling fell four percent from the previous day on Thursday. It was quoted at a commercial average of 70.2 against the dollar at 2 p.m. (1100 GMT), compared with 68.55 at 0730 GMT and a closing rate of 67.50 on Wednesday.
One bank quoted its selling rate at 71.50 against the dollar, while another quoted it at 71.15 as the Kenyan currency declined to its lowest levels for at least four years.

The Central Bank of Kenya lists the previous all-time low at 69.22 but commercial banks say a central bank instrument that put a premium on the dollar in October 1993 meant real market rates reached 83.
Floor dealers on the Nairobi Stock Exchange said bonds, in which foreign investors hold a huge stake, were under pressure, which was a major factor behind weakness of the shilling.
But brokers said market makers were now offering low prices on its Central Bank of Kenya floating rate treasury bonds to discourage foreign investors from pulling out.
"Foreign investors have contributed partly to the (shilling) problem by asking commercial banks to look for dollars and not in small amounts," a leading Nairobi bourse floor dealer said.
Commercial bank dealers said they were taking no chances and would maintain wide spreads to protect their trading positions.

"The shilling is still looking weak. Big orders are still there and since we're seeing support from the Central Bank of Kenya at top levels, we can only top it up," a senior dealer from a leading commercial bank told Reuters.

On Wednesday, Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem appealed to currency market operators to trade "in an orderly manner so that losses arising from the panic and speculative transactions would be minimised".
Commercial bank dealers said that despite the appeal, they could do little when the shilling was under intense pressure.
They said investors had been alarmed by President Daniel arap Moi playing down the IMF ruling and urging Kenyans to become self-reliant.
He also said the lost IMF loans under the soft-lending Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) were insignificant compared with Kenya's whole economy.

An opposition-backed coalition pressing for constitutional reforms has called a national strike for Friday. But some opposition groups have broken ranks, saying that dialogue ought to be given a chance.
